sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: 'Peace and security are inseparable.' Explain.
questions.answer: Peace cannot exist where people live under threat, and security is meaningless without harmony. Together they create a condition where individuals, institutions, nations and the world move ahead without threat; conflict creates fear and hampers progress.

questions.q: How does the new notion of security differ from the traditional notion? Give two points.
questions.answer: (1) The traditional notion is about military threats to a nation's territory and sovereignty; the new one covers threats like terrorism, hunger, disease, environmental damage and denial of human rights. (2) The new notion focuses on individuals and humankind, not just States, and treats security as a precondition of development and dignity.

questions.q: What contribution did the freedom movement make to India's approach to peace and security?
questions.answer: Leaders realised democracy and development need peace, pledged that free India would promote international peace, supported anti-colonial and anti-racist movements, and chose social justice and secularism to prevent internal threats.

questions.q: Why did India adopt the policy of non-alignment?
questions.answer: To keep its independence in foreign policy during the Cold War by not joining the US or Soviet military blocs, to judge each issue on merit, to promote world peace and to focus on its own development with help from all.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Why are peace and security essential for the progress of individuals, nations and the world? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) Development needs peace — no economic or social progress is possible amid violence or war; resources go to defence instead. (2) Democracy needs peace — elections, democratic institutions and people's participation can work only in peaceful conditions. (3) Individuals can live with dignity, free from fear, enjoy rights and plan their lives; at world level, peace allows trade and cooperation.

questions.q: Describe the strategy of the Government of India to deal with terrorism, insurgency and the Naxalite movement.
questions.answer: (1) Terrorism — support and seek international cooperation and put diplomatic pressure on Pakistan and neighbours to stop support to terrorist groups. (2) Insurgency — tackle it diplomatically through treaties with Myanmar and Bangladesh to stop help to insurgents, along with security measures. (3) Naxalism — treated as a socio-economic problem, not just law and order: speed up development in affected areas and bring youth into the mainstream.

questions.q: Explain the relationship between peace and security on one hand and democracy and development on the other.
questions.answer: (1) Without peace elections and democratic institutions cannot function and development cannot take place. (2) Democracies rarely go to war and give all citizens a chance to participate, removing causes of discontent. (3) Development improves quality of life and removes the sense of deprivation that leads to protests and violence; the 2005 World Summit called them interlinked and mutually reinforcing.

questions.q: What are the causes of the Naxalite movement? How can it be solved?
questions.answer: Causes: social discrimination and economic deprivation of tribals, SCs and dalits; the fruits of development not reaching them; disputes over land and forests. Solutions: faster development — roads, schools, jobs — in affected areas; land reforms and protection of forest rights; dialogue to bring youth into the mainstream along with firm action against violence.

questions.q: Explain any three basic objectives of India's foreign policy.
questions.answer: (1) Promotion of international peace and security and support to the United Nations. (2) Good relations with all nations, especially neighbours, while keeping freedom in policy formulation (non-alignment). (3) Disarmament; opposition to colonialism, imperialism and racism; and cooperation among developing nations.

questions.q: How has India supported the United Nations? Why does India deserve permanent membership of the Security Council?
questions.answer: Support: a founding member; contributes troops to UN peacekeeping; supports disarmament and settlement of disputes by negotiation; wants an active UN role in development of poor countries. Claim: largest democracy and huge population, fast-growing economy, long peacekeeping record and leadership of developing countries.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What is meant by peace and security? How is the traditional notion different from the new notion? Explain.
questions.answer: Peace is a condition of harmony ensuring development of individuals, society and the nation — not merely absence of war but presence of socio-cultural and economic understanding. Security is freedom from fear and dangerous threats, including threats to human rights. Traditional notion: (1) focuses on military threats from another nation; (2) concerns the nation's sovereignty and territory; (3) remedies are treaties, defence build-up, alliances and balance of power. New notion: (4) broader — terrorism, insurgency, genocide, epidemics, narcotics, environmental damage; (5) centred on individuals and humankind; (6) a precondition for development and human dignity — freedom from hunger, want, disease and exploitation.

questions.q: Examine the relevance of the Non-Aligned Movement and India's role in maintaining world peace through the UN.
questions.answer: NAM: (1) founded by Nehru, Tito and Nasser during the Cold War so new nations could stay free of military blocs; (2) after the Cold War it checks the dominance of a unipolar world; (3) it is a forum for North–South dialogue and South–South cooperation, raising the bargaining power of developing countries; (4) it presses for UN reform. UN: (5) India, a founding member, supports UN peacekeeping and disarmament and wants disputes solved by talks; (6) it seeks a UN role in development and a permanent seat in a reformed Security Council.
